study.title: 2 Chronicles 1 Solomon begins to reign with worship, prayer, and prosperity
study.overview: The chapter shows the consolidated beginning of Solomon's reign: God is with him, the people recognize him, and the king's first great decision is to seek the Lord in Gibeon, where the tabernacle of the testimony and the great bronze altar was. There Solomon offers sacrifices and receives from God the opportunity to ask whatever he desires. Instead of seeking personal advantages, he asks for wisdom and knowledge to rule a large people well. God approves this desire and adds riches, possessions and honor. Then the chapter describes the stability and greatness of the kingdom: chariots, knights, silver, gold, cedar wood and horse trade. The closure also suggests moral tension, because the accumulation of horses and trade with Egypt can be read in the light of the prohibition of Deuteronomy 17:16, even though the comment itself indicates discussion on the subject.

outline.title: Solomon is confirmed and seeks the Lord in Gibeon
outline.explanation: The chapter begins with the confirmation of Solomon's reign under the presence and blessing of God. He gathers leaders from all Israel and goes with them to Gibeon, because there was the tabernacle of the testimony and the bronze altar. The king offers a thousand burnt offerings, showing that his first concern is not political, but cultual.

outline.title: The Request for Wisdom and Divine Response
outline.explanation: That night, God speaks to Solomon and offers him what he asks. Solomon recognizes the mercy given to David and asks for wisdom and knowledge to rule and judge the people well. God approves the request because he did not seek wealth, glory or long life, and promises not only wisdom but also riches and honor.

outline.title: Prosperity of the kingdom and signs of possible tension
outline.explanation: Back in Jerusalem, Solomon rules with administrative and economic strength: he accumulates chariots, horsemen, silver, gold and wood in great abundance. Trade with Egypt and Coa brings horses and chariots to various kings. The text ends with a description of economic expansion, but this prosperity can be cautiously dealt with the old prohibition of multiplying horses.

study.context: The chapter relies on already known elements of the history of Israel: the tabernacle made by Moses, the bronze altar made by Bezalel, and the ark that David had brought to Jerusalem. Gibeon appears as the place where the tabernacle was still, while the ark was already in another tent prepared by David. The scenario indicates a transition between the desert heritage and the kingdom organized around Jerusalem, with Solomon at the beginning of his rule.
study.theology: The text presents a clear spiritual order: worship before government, dependence on God before human capacity. Solomon is shown as one who understands that true authority comes from the faithfulness of the Lord, and therefore asks for what best combines with his vocation: wisdom to administer justice. The divine answer teaches that God is pleased when the desires of the heart are aligned with the good of the people and with the task received. At the same time, material prosperity is not the center of the narrative; it comes as an addition, not as a target. The chapter also suggests that external success can coexist with risks of disobedience, so that God's blessing should not be confused with automatic approval of all that the king does.

scholarViews.insight: The commentaries note that Solomon's departure to Gibeon was a public event linked to the takeover of the throne, with military and tribal leaders, and that the place was chosen because there was the tabernacle and the bronze altar.
Matthew Henry notes that Solomon honored God first with sacrifice and prayer, and that he did not act as king before devoting himself to worship.
Adam Clarke points out that Solomon asked for wisdom and knowledge to rule well, understanding the verb used to administer or judge the people.

questions: What does Solomon's order worship before government teach about spiritual priorities and leadership today?
Why is God pleas more pleased with the request for wisdom than of requests for wealth, honor or long life?
In what ways can material success become a blessing received with gratitude or a moral danger if it departs from obedience?
study.practice: Before asking God for a solution to problems or increased resources, pray for wisdom to act with justice, discernment and humility. Also evaluate your own achievements: have they led you to serve God and people better, or to trust more material security? The chapter invites you to put the Lord at the centre of decisions, especially when there is power, responsibility and abundance.
study.uncertainty: There is an important interpretative observation at the end of the chapter: the mentions of horses, cars and trade with Egypt may indicate disobedience to the prohibition of multiplying horses, but this appears in the notes as a possibility and not as an unanimously closed conclusion. In addition, Coa's precise identity is not explained in the provided notes, so it is advisable to avoid statements beyond the text and comments data.
